Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u\\2 u^{2} + v^{2}\\- v\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(2 u^{2} + v^{2})&=4 u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(2 u^{2} + v^{2})&=2 v\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- v)&=-1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4 u\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2 v\\-1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1 & 4 u & 0\\0 & 2 v & -1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(4 u)(-1)\\&\quad -(0)(2 v)\\&=- 4 u.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(1)(-1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(1)(2 v)\\&\quad -(4 u)(0)\\&=2 v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}- 4 u\\1\\2 v\end{pmatrix}.
$$

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={2}^{2}\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}

Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $-1$ and a maximum value of $5$.

The midline is the horizontal line halfway between the minimum and maximum values. Average their heights:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{y_{\text{min}}+y_{\text{max}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{-1+5}{2} \\
&= 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=2$. The half-range $3$ is the amplitude, rather than the vertical shift.

Evaluate the surface integral

$$
\iint_S 4\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x + 2 y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2$.

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x + 2 y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x + 2 y)=2.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}4\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}4\sqrt{1+\left(1\right)^{2}+\left(2\right)^{2}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}4 \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A\\ & =4 \sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A\\ & =4 \sqrt{6}\cdot\text{Area}(D)\\ & =4 \sqrt{6}\cdot\left(1-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot\left(2-\left(0\right)\right)\\ & =4 \sqrt{6}\cdot\left(1\right)\cdot\left(2\right)\\ & =8 \sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Evaluate the surface integral

$$

$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\sin{\left(x + y \right)}$ for $0\le x\le \frac{3 \pi}{2}$ and $- x\le y\le x$.

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sin{\left(x + y \right)})=\cos{\left(x + y \right)},
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sin{\left(x + y \right)})=\cos{\left(x + y \right)}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{2 z}{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}}{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}\sqrt{1+\left(\cos{\left(x + y \right)}\right)^{2}+\left(\cos{\left(x + y \right)}\right)^{2}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}}{\cancel{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}}\cancel{\sqrt{2 \cos^{2}{\left(x + y \right)} + 1}}\,\text{d}A\\ & ={∬}_{D}2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}\,\text{d}A\\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\int_{- x}^{x}\left(2 \sin{\left(x + y \right)}\right)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}[- 2 \cos{\left(x + y \right)}]_{y=- x}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x\\ & =\int_{0}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\left(4 \sin^{2}{\left(x \right)}\right)\,\text{d}x\\ & =[(2 x)+(- \sin{\left(2 x \right)})]_{x=0}^{x=\frac{3 \pi}{2}}\\ & =\left((3 \pi)+(0)-\left((0)+(0)\right)\right)\\ & =3 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x + 4 y^{2}$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=-5\,i+2\,j.$

The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-5)^{2}+(2)^{2}}=\sqrt{29} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{29}}(-5\,i+2\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x + 4 y^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x + 4 y^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,8 y⟩ \\ ∇f(1,1) & =⟨1,8 (1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨1,8⟩\cdot ⟨- \frac{5 \sqrt{29}}{29},\frac{2 \sqrt{29}}{29}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(1)\cdot (-5)+(8)\cdot (2)}{\sqrt{29}} \\  & =\frac{11 \sqrt{29}}{29}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(2 - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &=8\left(1-\cos(t)\right) \\ &=16\sin^2\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

On the stated interval, $\sin\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\geq0$, so taking the square root gives

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2}=4 \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.
$$

Integrating, including the constant chain-rule factor, gives

$$
\int 4 \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t=- 8 \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}+C.
$$

Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}4 \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[- 8 \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \\ &=\left(-4\right)-\left(- 4 \sqrt{3}\right) \\ &=-4 + 4 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=2 y \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 x \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=1\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=2 x y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=2 x \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(0\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=2 x y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=h'(z).
$$

Comparing this derivative with the third component and subtracting the known terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}h'(z)&=1 \\ h(z)&=z+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

\begin{aligned}F(x,y,z)&=\left(2 y\right)\,\mathbf{i} \\ &{}+\left(2 x + z\right)\,\mathbf{j} \\ &{}+\left(y\right)\,\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=2 y \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=2 x + z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=y\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=2 x y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2 x + z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=2 x + z \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=y z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=2 x y + y z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=y+h'(z).
$$

Comparing this derivative with the third component and subtracting the known terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}h'(z)&=0 \\ h(z)&=C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=2 x y + y z+C.
$$
f(x,y,z)=- x y - y z - 2 z+C
f(x,y,z)=- x y + 2 y z + 2 z+C
f(x,y,z)=- x y + y z + z+C

The right side of the root equation is positive, so squaring is reversible. Exclude this level set. The radicand-zero boundary remains allowed wherever the numerator is real, since the denominator there is $-1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}&\oint_C\left(- 2 y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\&\quad+\left(x^{2} + x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The stated traversal is **counterclockwise**. Green's theorem applies because both coefficients have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$. For this orientation,

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y)&=- 2 y^{2},\\Q(x,y)&=x^{2} + x y.\end{aligned}
$$

Hold the other variable constant when taking each partial derivative. Apply the power rule to each relevant term.

$$

$$
